newsitem.title: USA: U.S. SEC adopts rules on market risk disclosure.
newsitem.headline: U.S. SEC adopts rules on market risk disclosure.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission adopted far-reaching rules on Tuesday that will require public companies to disclose more about the risks they take, including the use of derivatives.
Use of derivatives, financial instruments whose value is based on the value of another item, has skyrocketed in the past decade as a tool to manage risk.
But in some cases the often complex instruments have been blamed for causing huge, unexpected losses such as those Procter & Gamble Co and Gibson Greetings Inc suffered in 1994.

In a unanimous vote, the SEC agreed to require public companies to disclose descriptive and quantitative information about the potential for loss from derivatives or other holdings arising from changes in market prices or rates.

"Derivatives are like electricity -- dangerous if mishandled but also capable of doing enormous good," SEC chairman Arthur Levitt said, explaining the rationale for the rules. "Intelligent oversight can often make the crucial difference. An important oversight role is played by investors in our capital markets, who act as a check on significant decisions undertaken by management."

The rules will apply to annual financial statements filed after June 15, 1997, by all banks and thrifts, and companies with market capitalizations of over $2.5 billion, which includes about 500 of the largest public firms, SEC said.
All smaller companies, with the exception of registered investment companies and small business issuers, will have to abide by the rules beginning one year later.

In addition to derivatives holdings, other instruments that require disclosures include structured notes, loan receivables, debt obligations and deposit liabilities, the SEC said. Common stock holdings are excluded.
A company disclosing its market risks must choose among three alternatives for revealing the potential quantitative impact on earnings, cash flow or the balance sheet.
Companies with only a few derivatives would likely choose to present the estimated value and terms of each of their holdings in a simple table, SEC officials said.

Companies with more substantial holdings could show the estimated impact on their entire portfolio from hypothetical movements in interest rates or other relevent indicators. Or, companies could choose a measure known as "value at risk," which estimates the impact of recent historical market moves.
The SEC said it would reconsider the disclosure requirements within three years.
The new rules, 160 pages in all, drew quick criticism from some in the derivatives industry and Congress.
Rep. Michael Oxley, chairman of the House subcommittee that oversees the SEC, sent chairman Levitt a letter opposing the rules as burdensome and confusing.

"I am concerned that certain aspects of the proposed rule not only may fail to provide investors with more useful, intelligible information, but also may cause harm to American companies and their shareholders," the Ohio Republican wrote.
In an attempt to address some of the criticism, the SEC altered portions of the rules from an earlier proposal.

Some companies were concerned that the quantitative disclosures would reveal too much about their holdings and hedging strategies to competitors, especially to foreign competitors not subject to the rules.

In the final rules, SEC said companies may make disclosures based not only on their holdings at year end, but alternatively the average, high and low values during a year. Companies were also allowed to use different quantitative disclosure measures for different categories of holdings.
Derivatives dealers appeared unsatisfied with the changes, however.

"Corporate disclosures are improving so rapidly that shareholders today receive information that was not available to management five years ago," Gay Evans, chairman of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, said.
"As a result, locking in a specific standard today could inhibit the continuing evolution of risk management," added Evans, who is also senior managing director at Bankers Trust International.
--Aaron Pressman((202-898-8312))
